## What this package does

`styloprofile` measures how far a document sits from a statistical profile of human writing, rather
than training a human-vs-AI classifier. It describes typical writing with five interpretable
stylometric features (sentence length, conjunction use, variation in word length, syllable
complexity, vocabulary sophistication), summarises a reference corpus into a `stylo_profile`, and
scores new documents against it with two complementary distances. A high score means a document is
unusual *relative to the reference corpus* -- not evidence that it was machine-generated.

This vignette runs end to end using the two corpora bundled with the package, so it needs no
network access. For fetching a corpus of your own from OpenAlex, see `?fetch_corpus`.

```{r setup}
library(styloprofile)
```

## 1. The bundled corpora

`lidar_reference` and `lidar_contrast` are abstracts of lidar articles from one journal (IEEE
JSTARS), retrieved from OpenAlex and split by publication date: `lidar_reference` runs through the
end of 2022, `lidar_contrast` from 2023 onward.

```{r}
nrow(lidar_reference)
nrow(lidar_contrast)
lidar_reference$abstract[1]
```

## 2. Extracting the features directly

`build_profile()` calls this internally, but it's worth seeing what it computes on its own:

```{r}
stylo_features(lidar_reference$abstract[1:2])
```

## 3. Building a reference profile

```{r}
profile <- build_profile(lidar_reference$abstract)
profile
summary(profile)
```

`summary()` reports the covariance condition number -- how close the features are to collinear. A
large value means the distances are dominated by estimation noise in the smallest eigenvalue of the
covariance; `build_profile(x, shrink = 0.1)` shrinks the covariance toward a scaled identity matrix
to bring it down, at the cost of treating the features as slightly more independent than they are.

`plot()` draws the same `center`/`scale` table as one small panel per feature, since the features
differ too much in scale to share one axis:

```{r, fig.alt = "One panel per feature, each a point at the reference mean with whiskers at one reference standard deviation."}
plot(profile)
```

## 4. Scoring new documents

```{r}
scores <- score(lidar_contrast$abstract, profile, method = "mahalanobis")
scores
summary(scores)
```

`plot()` on a `stylo_score` draws a histogram of the scores with the same 95% flagging cut-off the
summary reports:

```{r, fig.alt = "A histogram of Mahalanobis distances with a dashed vertical line at the 95th-percentile cut-off."}
plot(scores)
```

The angular distance answers a different question -- not how extreme a document is, but whether the
*proportions* between its features are wrong, even when nothing is extreme:

```{r}
scores_angular <- score(lidar_contrast$abstract, profile, method = "angular")
summary(scores_angular)
```

## Interpreting the result

`lidar_contrast` is split from `lidar_reference` by publication date, not by authorship, so a
raised score here is a distributional shift across time, not a measure of detection accuracy. Two of
the five features, `vocab_sophistication` and `mean_sentence_length`, also correlate with English
proficiency and education, so a non-native English speaker writing ordinary prose can sit far from a
profile built from native, highly educated writers. A flagged document is a statistical outlier
relative to the reference corpus it was scored against, and nothing more -- the choice of reference
corpus has to be documented wherever a verdict is reported.
